question: A 55-year-old man presents with sudden-onset severe central abdominal pain that rapidly becomes generalised. His abdomen is board-like and he has free gas under the diaphragm on erect chest X-ray. This is best classified as:

answers.text: Primary (spontaneous) peritonitis — haematogenous spread of organisms in the absence of an intra-abdominal source

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Primary peritonitis occurs without a visceral perforation, most often in patients with ascites or immunosuppression. Free gas under the diaphragm indicates a perforated hollow viscus — a secondary cause.

answers.text: Secondary peritonitis — due to perforation of a hollow viscus (here, likely perforated peptic ulcer)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Free subdiaphragmatic gas confirms perforation of a hollow viscus — the commonest cause of secondary peritonitis. Sudden generalised peritonism with a board-like abdomen clinches the presentation.

answers.text: Tertiary peritonitis — persistent or recurrent infection after adequate treatment of secondary peritonitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tertiary peritonitis is a late complication in ICU patients who fail to resolve secondary peritonitis. This is a first acute presentation with free gas.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key point: free gas under the diaphragm = perforation = secondary peritonitis. Primary peritonitis has no visceral perforation; tertiary peritonitis is a late ICU complication.
Correct. Free gas + board-like abdomen = secondary peritonitis from hollow-viscus perforation — emergency laparotomy is the priority.
